lead: Branch, jump and call instructions change the program counter (PC), the register that holds the address of the next instruction. A jump replaces the PC with a target address. A conditional jump does that only when a flag matches, so the CPU can choose between paths after a compare. A call also saves a return address on the stack, so RET can come back. These control transfer instructions build if-then logic, loops and subroutines in every 8085, 8086 and 8051 program.
prereq: You need: flags from 3.4 and the program counter from Unit 2.

blocks.text: An unconditional jump always changes the PC. The 8085 JMP addr loads addr. The 8086 JMP may be SHORT (8-bit displacement), NEAR (same code segment) or FAR (new CS:IP). The 8051 has SJMP (relative, -128 to +127 bytes), AJMP (absolute inside a 2 KB page) and LJMP (16-bit absolute). A relative target is measured from the instruction after the jump; an absolute target is the full address carried in the instruction. Some syllabi call these control transfer instructions.

A conditional jump tests flags set by an earlier instruction, often CMP. CMP subtracts operands and sets flags but stores no result. Z is the zero flag, C is carry, S is sign and P is parity. On the 8085, JZ jumps if Z = 1; JNZ if Z = 0; JC if C = 1; JNC if C = 0; JP if S = 0; JM if S = 1; JPE if P = 1; JPO if P = 0. On the 8086, JS/JNS are the usual sign jumps and JP/JNP (or JPE/JPO) test parity; assemblers may accept older aliases. Check the mnemonic against the CPU: on the 8085 JP tests S = 0 (positive) and JPE tests parity, while on the 8086 JP and JPE both mean parity even and the sign jumps are JS/JNS.

The 8051 is different: JZ jumps when accumulator A is zero, and JNZ jumps when A is not zero. CJNE compares and jumps if not equal, and sets C = 1 if the first operand is below the second unsigned. DJNZ decrements a register and jumps if it is not zero.

A call is a jump that remembers where to return. The CPU loads the target into PC and pushes the return address, the address of the instruction after CALL, on the stack. RET pops that address back into PC. On the 8085, CALL pushes the 16-bit PC. On the 8086, a near call pushes only IP; a far call pushes CS and IP. The 8051 LCALL pushes the 16-bit PC, and ACALL is a 2 KB page call. Use a call for reusable code; see 3.6 for stack details.

LOOP is a counted jump. 8086 LOOP decrements CX and jumps to the label if CX ≠ 0. If CX = 0 it falls through. 8051 DJNZ does the same with any register: DJNZ R2, label. A loop body runs once for each starting count, and the register ends at 0.

Near and far calls differ in stack use. A near target is in the same segment. A far target has a new segment and offset. A RET must match the call type; a far RET pops CS and IP. A wrong RET corrupts the stack.

A relative jump stores a small signed displacement d. The CPU computes the target from the next instruction, not from the jump's own address. Example: at 1000H, an 8051 SJMP with d = +05H jumps to 1007H, because the instruction is 2 bytes, so the next address is 1002H and 1002H + 5 = 1007H. The range is -128 to +127 bytes, so relative code is compact and movable.

blocks.where: d is the signed displacement in bytes; next instruction address is the address after the jump instruction.

blocks.text: An absolute jump stores the full target. AJMP stores 11 address bits (A10-A0) and takes the upper 5 bits from the address of the next instruction, so the target must lie in the same 2 KB page as the instruction after the AJMP. LJMP stores all 16 bits. The 8086 SHORT jump stores an 8-bit displacement and the NEAR jump a 16-bit displacement, both counted from the address of the next instruction, so both are relative. A FAR jump carries a full CS:IP address and is absolute. Choose relative for nearby code and absolute for fixed addresses such as interrupt vectors.

figure.caption: CMP B subtracts 07H from 05H; the borrow sets C = 1, so JC LESS is taken and the next instruction is skipped.

spec.title: JC after CMP
spec.aria: CMP B sets C = 1 from 05H minus 07H, so the JC LESS path is taken and the normal next instruction is skipped.

examples.question: 8085 program: A = 05H and B = 07H. Execute CMP B, then JC LESS. State the flags and whether the jump is taken.
steps: CMP B computes A - B, that is 05H - 07H.
05H = 5 and 07H = 7. The subtraction 5 - 7 needs a borrow, so the 8-bit result is 5 - 7 + 256 = 254 = FEH.
CMP does not change A. It sets flags from FEH and from the borrow.
C = 1 because a borrow was needed. Z = 0 because FEH is not 00H. S = 1 because bit 7 of FEH is 1.
JC tests C. Since C = 1, the jump to LESS is taken. If C = 0, control would fall through.
examples.answer: A remains 05H; C = 1, Z = 0, S = 1; JC LESS is taken.
examples.check:
a=0x05
b=0x07
res=(a-b)&0xFF
c=1 if a<b else 0
z=1 if res==0 else 0
s=(res>>7)&1
print(a)
print(b)
print(res)
print(c)
print(z)
print(s)

traps: CMP sets flags only; it does not store the subtraction result, so A is unchanged.
After CMP on unsigned bytes, JC means A < B. For signed numbers, carry alone is not enough; sign and overflow must also be checked.
CALL is not a jump. CALL pushes a return address; JMP does not. A RET after a JMP pops a wrong value.
A relative displacement is counted from the instruction after the jump, not from the jump's own address.
8085 JZ tests the Z flag; 8051 JZ tests accumulator A. 8086 LOOP decrements CX before testing, so CX = 0 gives 65536 passes.

quiz.q: What does CALL do to the PC and the stack?
quiz.a: CALL loads the target address into the PC and pushes the return address, the address of the instruction after CALL, on the stack.

quiz.q: Why does JZ after CMP test equality for unsigned bytes?
quiz.a: CMP subtracts and sets Z = 1 when the result is 00H, which happens when the operands are equal; JZ then tests Z.

quiz.q: 8085: A = FFH, B = 01H. Execute CMP B, then JC LESS. State C, Z, S and whether the jump is taken.
quiz.a: FFH - 01H = FEH; no borrow so C = 0; result not zero so Z = 0; bit 7 = 1 so S = 1; JC tests C = 0, so the jump is not taken.

quiz.q: A student replaces CALL SUB with JMP SUB. Why does the program fail when SUB ends with RET?
quiz.a: JMP does not push a return address; RET pops an old or wrong value into the PC, so control does not return to the instruction after the call.

quiz.q: Give one difference between a relative jump and an absolute jump.
quiz.a: A relative jump stores a signed displacement from the next instruction; an absolute jump stores the full target address.

quiz.q: 8086: CX = 3 before LOOP AGAIN. How many times does the body run and what is CX after the loop?
quiz.a: The body runs 3 times; LOOP decrements CX after each pass and stops when CX = 0, so final CX = 0.

quiz.q: Why can the same JZ mnemonic behave differently on 8085 and 8051?
quiz.a: 8085 JZ tests the Z flag set by earlier arithmetic; 8051 JZ tests only accumulator A for zero.

quiz.q: 8051: R2 = 02H. How many times does DJNZ R2, AGAIN execute its body?
quiz.a: Two times; after the second decrement R2 = 0, so the jump is not taken.

beyond: Not for the exam. Modern CPUs add branch predictors to guess whether a conditional jump is taken, and a wrong guess costs pipeline cycles. Indirect calls and returns use a return-address stack. RISC designs often keep the return address in a link register; ARM uses BL. Search for branch prediction, return-address stack and delayed branch.
